notes:
I only got through part of the research before running out of tool calls, so these notes come from a small set of pages:
- **Read in full:** Wesley's Notes, plus the Bible Hub page on 6:53 (Ellicott, Matthew Henry, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Poole and Gill).
- **Seen only as search snippets:** catholic.com, desiringgod.org and gotquestions.org.
- **Not read at all:** Enduring Word/Guzik, Pulpit, Precept Austin, any Lutheran site (lcms.org, 1517.org), Orthodox (oca.org), NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, and anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Gill, Ellicott and the others are covered only at v. 53.

Verses I found nothing on are left out.

---

**v. 48–49:** No comments found apart from Wesley's note on v. 31. There he says the manna came from the "lower" sky, while Jesus came from the highest heaven. Wesley counts seven places in the chapter (vv. 32, 33, 38, 50, 58, 62) where Jesus says he came down from heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 50:** Wesley: "not die" means not die spiritually or eternally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 51:** Wesley takes eating this bread to mean believing in Jesus. The person who believes to the end will be saved. He says the whole teaching about flesh and blood points directly to Jesus' suffering and death, and to the Lord's Supper "but remotely, if at all." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm
- *Catholic view:* catholic.com notes that Jesus speaks in the future tense here ("the bread which I shall give"). It reads John 6 as a promise that was fulfilled at the Last Supper, where Jesus commands what he promised here. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/if-you-eat-my-flesh-you-eat-my-body

**v. 52:** Wesley sees three stages of testing in the passage: first the Jews (here), then the disciples (vv. 60–66), then the apostles (v. 67). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm
- *Catholic view:* Catholic Answers says the listeners understood Jesus literally—and correctly, and that he did not correct these protesters. https://www.catholic.com/tract/christ-in-the-eucharist

**v. 53:** This is the key verse where readings split. All of the following are on https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/6-53.htm unless another link is given.
- **Ellicott:** The Old Testament forbids eating blood in seven places, so the hearers would have been horrified. Mentioning blood separately from flesh points to Jesus' death. The spiritual meaning is taking his atonement into your inmost self.
- **Matthew Henry:** Eating this flesh and drinking this blood means believing in Christ. We share in Christ and his benefits by faith.
- **Barnes:** Jesus did not mean this literally, and the passage is not about the Lord's Supper, which had not yet been set up. It means that through his sacrificial death Jesus wins pardon and life for people. Barnes argues directly against the Catholic teaching from the Council of Trent.
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** This was the harshest thing Jesus had said to them yet. "Drink his blood" would have suggested his death. The point is that people must take his sacrificial death as their own, so that it becomes the life of their inner self.
- **Poole:** Mentions two old debates:
  1. Lutherans and Calvinists disagreed over whether Christ's human nature itself gives life. Poole says the Lutherans held that it does, because it is united to his divine nature.
  2. Against Catholics, Poole says that Protestants, "both Lutherans and Calvinists," deny that this passage is about the sacrament.

  This is Poole describing the Lutherans, not a Lutheran writer speaking for himself.
- **Gill:** Eating means feeding on Christ by faith, not physical eating. The verse is not about the Lord's Supper. Gill adds that reading it as being about the Supper once led to giving communion to infants.
- **Wesley:** Eating is "spiritually" drawing constant strength from Christ by faith. It is "only another expression for believing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm
- **Desiring God (Baptist):** Christians have misread these verses for 2,000 years, and Catholic transubstantiation grew out of that. The article's heading is "Eating Is Believing." https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/my-flesh-is-true-food
- **GotQuestions:** Jesus was using picture language, and we must receive Him by faith. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jesus-eat-flesh-drink-blood.html
- **Catholic view:** Catholic Answers argues that among Jews, the phrase "eat the flesh and drink the blood" used as a figure of speech meant doing someone serious harm, especially by slander. So, it says, a purely symbolic reading doesn't work. https://www.catholic.com/tract/christ-in-the-eucharist
- **Catholic answer to the cannibalism objection:** Catholics receive the whole, living, glorified Christ, not his dead flesh. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/are-catholics-wrong-about-john-6-part-i

**v. 54:**
- **Ellicott:** The Greek verb used here means to eat eagerly, with pleasure. The promise is the same one made earlier to those who "behold," "come" and "believe." https://biblehub.com/john/6-53.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Quotes Edersheim, who sees a double meaning: Jesus' death, and the Christian sacrament that celebrates it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/6-53.htm
- **Vincent:** Eating the flesh means taking his life as your own. Drinking the blood means taking the saving merit of his death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/6-53.htm

**v. 55:**
- **Wesley:** The believer's soul is fed by Christ as truly as the body is fed by food. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm
- **Catholic view:** "I am the door" and "I am the vine" make sense as metaphors, but v. 55 goes beyond symbolism. https://www.catholic.com/tract/christ-in-the-eucharist

**v. 57:** Wesley: Jesus lives by the Father because he is one with him. The believer lives by Jesus because he is one with Jesus. He calls this an "amazing union." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 58:** Wesley: Jesus is the bread, unlike the manna, whose eaters died anyway. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 60:** Wesley: the saying is hard for worldly people but sweet to God's children. Jesus rarely spoke more loftily, even to the apostles in private. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 62:** Wesley: if they saw him go up to heaven, it would seem even harder to believe that he could give them his flesh to eat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 63:** Another verse where readings split.
- **Wesley:** "The flesh" means the bare, literal meaning, which is no help. Jesus' words are meant spiritually, and understood that way they bring life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm
- **GotQuestions:** Jesus says this to show he has been speaking in metaphor. It argues that transubstantiation and the "consubstantiation" it says some Lutherans hold both ignore this verse. That description of Lutherans is GotQuestions' own, not a Lutheran source. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jesus-eat-flesh-drink-blood.html
- **Catholic view:** Jesus said "the flesh," not "my flesh," profits nothing. He would not call his own flesh useless after saying it would be given for the life of the world. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/is-the-eucharist-truly-jesus-body-and-blood

**v. 64:** Wesley: those who don't believe get no life from Jesus' words because they take them crudely and literally. The verse shows God foresees future free choices, but his knowing ahead of time does not cause the wrongdoing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 65:** This verse touches on a Calvinist vs. Wesleyan difference, but I only have the Wesleyan side. Wesley says coming to Christ is given only to those who will receive it on God's own terms. On v. 44 he calls God's drawing "resistible," not forced. I didn't read any Reformed source on this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 66:**
- **Wesley:** Jesus was beginning to sift his followers. The proud and careless left. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm
- **Catholic view:** These disciples left because they still took his words literally. That is why Catholic Answers argues Jesus wasn't "clearing up" a misunderstanding in v. 63. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/is-the-eucharist-truly-jesus-body-and-blood

**v. 68:** Wesley: Jesus alone speaks the words that show the way to eternal life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 69:** Wesley: the Twelve, who had been with Jesus from the start, were fully sure he is the Christ. His note follows the KJV wording ("that Christ, the Son of the living God"), not the BSB's "Holy One of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 70:** Wesley: the Twelve were chosen, but they could still fall away from that choosing. Judas should have repented at this kind warning. "Is a devil" means he was already under a devil's influence. This fits Wesley's note on v. 39: those given to Christ are kept "if they endure to the end. But Judas did not." I found no Reformed source to compare. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/6.htm

**v. 59, 61, 67, 71:** No comments found.

---

**Next places to look:** Guzik on John 6 (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/guzik/john/6.htm); the full Ellicott, Gill, Calvin and Pulpit chapters (links are on the 6:53 page above); Lutheran writers on lcms.org or 1517.org for the Lutheran reading in their own words; oca.org for the Orthodox view; and NET Bible notes on vv. 53 and 63.
